rv.q: Actually, it’s more like three – making it a 360, all-round, head-spinning winner.
But it made me laugh out loud more often than just about anything else I’ve seen in the last 12 months and the characters are charming and winningly delineated.
It is impossible not to be swept along by the giddily escalating mirth of Matt DiCarlo’s amiable production...
I’d say it takes near genius to fashion something this incorrigibly goofy.
For bungling wit matched with peerless physical comedy, you'd be hard pressed to find better in the West End.
I was crying helpless tears of laughter within the first five minutes, and at several other moments throughout.
Lewis... steals scene after scene as Douglas Woodbead, a monumentally self-satisfied thespian.
It can feel as if five shows’ worth of slapstick and farce has been crammed into one, which is a mixed blessing.
But while the physical comedy is impeccably executed, the bare-bones story it’s running on will leave some craving a little more substance.
Farce this slick, this tongue-in-cheek, this quirkily British, will always draw laughter from a hugely appreciative audience.
Mischief is a creative, comedic powerhouse, and the clever storyline and talented cast make The Comedy About Spies not only a spectacular spy spoof but also an outstanding show altogether.
If you are new to their style, it’s a fabulous introduction.

The Comedy About Spies is wonderful stuff, and highly amusing: this is a production company that has honed their craft, and their experience shines through in what is probably their most sophisticated show yet, at least in its technical aspects.
Their latest show, an espionage spoof, improvised and scripted, strong on wordplay, is as silly and as funny and as absurd as their past productions.
What could easily have come off the rails is majestically held together by Matt DiCarlo’s razor-sharp direction.
This is an evening of daft, uncomplicated fun.
This is clearly going to be an enormous popular hit.
Without a doubt, the funniest show I have seen in years and the funniest show I’d expect anyone to see this year.
The brilliant minds of Mischief have done it again, delivering another incredibly clever slapstick comedy that will have you laughing until you can’t breathe.
This latest addition to Mischief’s catalogue is a shining example of perfectly executed farce and uproarious theatrical chaos.
This finely tuned machine of comic timing and theatrical chaos is possibly Mischief’s best work yet, offering audiences exactly what they have come to expect – and love – from this troupe.
The Comedy About Spies is more than just a comedy; it's a masterclass in theatrical entertainment.
This show will keep you chuckling.
A delightfully daft show filled to the brim with laughs, I dare say that The Comedy About Spies is among Mischief Theatre's best works.
Their latest West End show, The Comedy About Spies, is another absolute masterclass in blending quick-fire wit, physical comedy, and theatrical mayhem.
Mischief at their best, as finely worked as clockwork and exuberant as toddlers.
The Comedy About Spies is an absolutely stellar show from its production to its performance, and certainly a strong contender for best watch of the year.
It’s sharp, silly, impeccably performed, and laugh-out-loud hilarious.
The scriptwriting, the set design, the acting, everything comes together to produce an excellent comedy with great twists at the end.
The Comedy About Spies delivers with all the Mischief Theatre charm with clever writing, witty and playful humour and fantastic acting.

Mischief take on a fresh genre to parody in The Comedy About Spies that does a good job of combining the company’s classic style of comedy with a heartfelt and intriguing plot, making for an entertaining couple of hours in the theatre.
A riot from start to finish, minutely planned, plotted and executed, with blisteringly good performances and every opportunity taken to make you laugh.

Equal parts side-splittingly funny and gasp-worthy, the play (that definitely went right) truly goes above and beyond expectations, a creative stroke of genius in what can be accomplished in a comedy play.
The show's worth seeing for this 'pre-credits' sequence alone, but do stick around for the rest of it.

cn.t: Mischief Theatre delivers another farcical hit with this 1960s spy spoof, earning praise for its clever wordplay, precise physical comedy, and chaotic energy, though some critics find the formula wearing thin and the humor insubstantial.
